quests.instruction: Draw a square: four sides of equal length and four sharp corners.
quests.hint: Go down, across, up, and across to close it. Make each side about the same length and turn at each corner without rounding it.
quests.explanation: A square needs four sharp turns. Learning to change direction at a corner is important for letters like E, F and H.
quests.funFact: A square has the same length on all four sides, while a rectangle only needs its opposite sides to match.

quests.instruction: Draw a triangle: slant up, slant down, then close it along the bottom.
quests.hint: Start at the bottom left, slant up to the point, slant down to the right, then pull back along the bottom to where you began.
quests.explanation: A triangle uses two slants and one flat line. These three strokes show up again in capital A.
quests.funFact: Triangles are very strong shapes, which is why you see them inside bridges and roof frames.

quests.instruction: Draw a square and put a triangle beside it, like the parts of a little house.
quests.hint: Draw the square first, then the triangle at the same height. Keep both shapes about the same size.
quests.explanation: Switching between straight-sided and slanted shapes gets your hand ready for letters that mix both.
quests.funFact: Each face of an Egyptian pyramid is a triangle.

quests.instruction: Draw a diamond: start at the top point and slant down to each side, then to the bottom point.
quests.hint: Slant down-left, then down-right to the bottom, then up-right and up-left. Aim for four pointed corners.
quests.explanation: A diamond is made from four slants that meet at points. Slants meeting neatly is how letters like V and X look sharp.
quests.funFact: A deck of playing cards has four suits: hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.

quests.instruction: Draw a rectangle that is longer than it is tall.
quests.hint: Draw a long line across, a short line down, another long line back, and a short line up. Make the long sides match.
quests.explanation: A rectangle trains you to make two different lengths, long and short, in the right places.
quests.funFact: A sheet of A4 paper is a rectangle about 21 centimeters wide and 29.7 centimeters tall.

quests.instruction: Draw a square, a rectangle and a diamond in a row.
quests.hint: Plan the space first: three shapes in a row, each with a small gap. Finish one shape before the next.
quests.explanation: Planning space for several shapes in a row is exactly what you do when you write letters across a page.
quests.funFact: Paper was invented in ancient China, long before it reached Europe.

quests.instruction: Draw an arrow pointing right: a line from left to right, then a small point at the end.
quests.hint: Draw the line left to right. At the end, make a short slant back and down, and another back and up, like a tiny roof.
quests.explanation: Arrows teach direction. Knowing which way your pen travels is the first step to writing letters correctly.
quests.funFact: In Egyptian hieroglyphs, the animal and people signs face the direction in which the line should be read.

quests.instruction: Draw an arrow pointing down: a line from top to bottom, then a small point at the end.
quests.hint: Pull straight down first. At the bottom, add two short slants going up and out to make the arrow head.
quests.explanation: Down arrows rehearse the same top-to-bottom pull as the stem of many letters.
quests.funFact: On a keyboard, the arrow keys move the cursor around the screen.

quests.instruction: Draw a path: an arrow right, an arrow down, and an arrow left, in order.
quests.hint: Say the directions as you draw: right, down, left. Give each arrow the same size.
quests.explanation: Changing direction on purpose, and in order, is what you do inside every letter and every line of writing.
quests.funFact: A compass needle is a small magnet that points toward the north.

quests.instruction: Make one neat dot: press your pen down and lift it straight away.
quests.hint: Touch the paper lightly and lift. Do not slide the pen, or the dot will turn into a tiny line.
quests.explanation: A dot is a perfect start-and-stop. Knowing exactly where your pen lands is the heart of careful writing.
quests.funFact: The dot above the letters i and j has its own name: it is called a tittle.

quests.instruction: Make three dots in a row with equal spaces between them.
quests.hint: Place the first dot, move about a thumb-width, and place the next. Keep them all on the same level.
quests.explanation: Placing dots at equal distances trains your eyes to measure space, which you will need between letters and words.
quests.funFact: Three dots in a row are called an ellipsis, and they show that something is missing or continues.

quests.instruction: Draw a line that starts exactly on one dot and ends exactly on the next.
quests.hint: Put your pen on the left dot, glide across, and stop right on the second dot. Do not go past it.
quests.explanation: Starting and stopping on target is called precision. Letters join and close properly only when strokes end where they should.
quests.funFact: The painter Georges Seurat made whole pictures from tiny dots of color, a style called pointillism.

quests.instruction: Copy this pattern: across, down, across, down. Keep going to the end.
quests.hint: Say 'across, down' as you draw. Let every down-stroke be the same height.
quests.explanation: Repeating a pattern keeps your pen moving in a steady rhythm, with each stroke matching the one before.
quests.funFact: People in many cultures weave patterns of lines into cloth, baskets and mats.

quests.instruction: Draw a fence: a standing post, then a slanted rail, over and over.
quests.hint: Draw the post, then a slant that starts from its bottom and rises. Make every post the same height.
quests.explanation: Mixing a straight line and a slanted line in a pattern is practice for letters like k and N.
quests.funFact: The word 'fence' is short for 'defence', since fences were first built to protect.

quests.instruction: Copy this pattern of plus signs joined by short lines, neatly and evenly.
quests.hint: Make each plus first, then the short joining line. Check the spaces are equal before you start the next.
quests.explanation: Patterns with joins ask your hand to plan ahead. Planning stroke order makes handwriting faster.
quests.funFact: Dominoes have patterns of dots called pips, and each tile has two ends.

quests.instruction: Draw three pairs of curves facing each other, like hugging brackets.
quests.hint: Draw each pair separately: left curve, then right curve. Leave a slightly bigger gap between pairs.
quests.explanation: Pairs of curves train you to repeat a shape and also to leave space between groups.
quests.funFact: Brackets and parentheses are used in math to show which part to calculate first.

quests.instruction: Draw an up-curve, a down-curve, an up-curve and a down-curve, all in a row.
quests.hint: Alternate: over the top, under the bottom. Keep all four of the same height and width.
quests.explanation: Switching between curve directions without stopping is the first taste of flowing, joined writing.
quests.funFact: A bouncing ball makes arcs as it goes, and each bounce is usually lower than the last.

quests.instruction: Draw two curves with a small circle between them.
quests.question: ( o )
quests.hint: First the left curve, then the little circle in the middle, then the right curve. Keep the circle centered.
quests.explanation: Fitting a small shape inside a space between two others means you must plan the sizes in advance.
quests.funFact: A bullseye target is made of circles inside circles, all sharing the same center.

quests.instruction: Draw a spiral: start in the middle and circle outward, getting bigger each time.
quests.hint: Begin with a tiny circle in the center, then widen it a little with every turn. Go counter-clockwise.
quests.explanation: A spiral keeps your pen moving in one smooth curve. Smooth curves make round letters look natural.
quests.funFact: A snail's shell grows in a spiral as the snail gets bigger.

quests.instruction: Draw two circles that touch side by side, like a pair of glasses.
quests.question: OO
quests.hint: Draw the first circle, then place the second so it just touches. Keep both the same size.
quests.explanation: Controlling where one shape ends and the next begins is a skill you use whenever letters sit side by side.
quests.funFact: Eyeglasses were invented in Italy more than 700 years ago.

quests.instruction: Draw three circles joined by short lines, like beads on a string.
quests.question: O-O-O
quests.hint: Draw circle, line, circle, line, circle. The joining lines should be level and the same length.
quests.explanation: Joining shapes with a short, level line is practice for connecting letters in a word.
quests.funFact: The five rings of the Olympic Games are linked together to show the coming together of athletes from around the world.

quests.instruction: Draw a valley: slant down to a point, then slant up again.
quests.question: V
quests.hint: Go down-right to the bottom point, then up-right. Make both slants about the same length.
quests.explanation: A pointed corner needs a small stop at the bottom before you change direction. Capital V uses exactly this shape.
quests.funFact: V is the Roman numeral for 5.

quests.instruction: Draw a peak: slant up to a point, then slant down again.
quests.hint: Go up-right to the top point, then straight down-right. Keep both sides even.
quests.explanation: A peak is a valley flipped upside down. Seeing shapes both ways builds understanding of letters like A and M.
quests.funFact: On a keyboard, the ^ mark is called a caret.

quests.instruction: Draw a valley, a peak and a valley again, with a small space between each.
quests.question: V ^ V
quests.hint: Check where each shape starts. All three should sit on the same level with equal gaps.
quests.explanation: Pointed shapes next to each other make you plan where to start. Neat starting points lead to neat lines.
quests.funFact: The sharp point where two lines meet is called a vertex.

quests.instruction: Draw five short lines in a row, each one resting right on the bottom line.
quests.hint: Rest your pen right on the bottom line and slide across. If you float above it, the line looks like it is flying.
quests.explanation: Letters sit on a baseline like toys on a shelf. Resting every stroke on it keeps writing tidy.
quests.funFact: Musical notes sit on a set of five lines called a staff.

quests.instruction: Draw standing lines joined by short lines at the bottom, like a row of small steps.
quests.hint: Stand each line on the baseline, then slide the little base line to the next. Keep every step the same width.
quests.explanation: Going from a tall stroke to the baseline and then across makes your hand practice stopping on the line.
quests.funFact: Early writing teachers in Europe used a sharp tool to rule faint lines on parchment so writing stayed straight.

quests.instruction: Draw a row of mountains that all sit on the baseline.
quests.hint: Slant up to the peak and slant down to the line, then slide along it. Make every peak the same height.
quests.explanation: Peaks of equal height sitting on the baseline need careful judging of both size and position, as in handwriting.
quests.funFact: Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level on Earth.

quests.instruction: Draw these four strokes in order, from memory: a standing line, a sleeping line, an uphill slant and a downhill slant.
quests.hint: Say the names quietly as you go: down, across, up-slant, down-slant. Start each from its correct point.
quests.explanation: These four strokes are the building blocks of many capital letters. Recalling them from memory shows they are in your hand now.
quests.funFact: Many letters in the Roman alphabet can be made from just straight lines and curves.

quests.instruction: Draw a circle, a plus and a cross in order. Try to make them equal in size.
quests.question: O + X
quests.hint: Circle from the top and move left, plus is down then across, cross is two slants. Match sizes as you go.
quests.explanation: Switching between a round shape and two crossing shapes shows your hand can change plans smoothly.
quests.funFact: The letter O is shaped like a circle because it came from an ancient picture of an eye.

quests.instruction: Draw a square, a triangle and a circle in a row, leaving equal gaps.
quests.question: □ △ O
quests.hint: Look at the space across the page and plan three equal spots. Draw each shape completely before moving on.
quests.explanation: Spacing shapes evenly is the same job you do between letters in a word. You are ready to start real letters.
quests.funFact: The alphabet we use today came to English through the Romans, who borrowed from the Greeks, who borrowed from the Phoenicians.
